Formulation
- Predisposing factors: personal history of anxiety; family history of anxiety (mother).
- Precipitating factors: increased work pressure and backlog over the past ~2 months, late nights prior to presentation.
- Perpetuating factors: ongoing late nights, inadequate sleep, possible inadequate hydration and fatigue (clinician noted these as potential contributors).
- Protective factors: partner support, regular exercise, ongoing SSRI (Sertraline), willingness to engage with recommended interventions (analgesia, rest, counseling) and follow-up.
- Summary: Acute unilateral headache likely related to either migraine or tension-type mechanisms, with situational work stress and disturbed sleep contributing. Anxiety history may predispose to tension-type headache; dehydration/fatigue were considered possible exacerbating factors.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute unilateral headache (possible migraine vs tension-type)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Agreed to try recommended measures and review in one week
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Reduce current headache pain and frequency; differentiate migraine vs tension-type if not improved; identify and address contributing factors (sleep, hydration, stress)
- Actions (Patient):
  - Take analgesia as recommended (Paracetamol already taken; clinician recommended starting Ibuprofen) — dose/route/frequency not documented
  - Rest/lie down as needed; attempt to obtain adequate sleep (target 7–8 hours/night)
  - Increase fluid intake to approximately 1.5–2 liters/day (excluding coffee/tea)
  - Consider taking a period off work (self-certify for ~1 week) to reduce stress
  - Book and attend follow-up appointment in one week; return earlier if symptoms worsen or new concerning signs develop
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Recommended ibuprofen for migraine-type headache (dose/route/frequency not documented)
  - Advised continuing or using Paracetamol as needed
  - Provided advice on sleep hygiene, hydration, and rest
  - Will provide a link to information on headache red flags/danger signs
  - Arrange 1-week follow-up; consider blood tests or further evaluation if no improvement or if concerning features develop
  - Low threshold to reassess earlier if patient deteriorates

Secondary Problem: Anxiety disorder (history)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Continue current management; address situational anxiety relating to workload; engage with counseling services
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Maintain stability on Sertraline; reduce work-related anxiety symptoms; provide access to psychological support
- Actions (Patient):
  - Continue Sertraline as per current prescription (dose not documented)
  - Self-refer to counseling service using the link to be provided
  - Continue regular exercise (running ~3x/week) as tolerated
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Document ongoing Sertraline treatment (dose/route/frequency not documented)
  - Provide counseling service link for self-referral
  - Monitor anxiety symptoms at follow-up; escalate care if worsening or if new risk emerges

Tertiary Problem: Work-related stress and sleep disruption
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Reduce workload-related stress and improve sleep quantity/quality
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Implement short-term stress-reduction measures; improve sleep hygiene
- Actions (Patient):
  - Consider self-certifying time off work for approximately one week
  - Implement sleep hygiene measures (target 7–8 hours/night)
  - Increase fluids; reduce late nights where possible
  - Engage with counseling for coping strategies
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Advise on and support short-term time off (self-certification)
  - Provide counseling referral information and follow-up appointment
  - Reassess at 1-week follow-up and consider further interventions (e.g., referral to specialist, investigations) if symptoms persist

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Differential of tension-type headache vs migraine, recommended acute analgesia options (ibuprofen preferred over paracetamol per clinician), role of sleep and hydration in headaches, counseling options, and written information/link to headache red flags/danger signs
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Not documented verbatim in transcript; clinician to provide written link to danger signs (patient advised to read and use this)
- Coping Strategies:
  - Rest/lying down when symptomatic, acute analgesia (ibuprofen/paracetamol), adequate sleep (7–8 hours), maintain hydration (1.5–2 L/day), consider time off work, engage in counseling, continue regular exercise
